request: a which-came-first history game where you guess which of two events happened earlier

brief.intent: a brainy chronology quiz with surprising pairs

themes: history timeline dates which came first chronology trivia science inventions
why_its_good: Every pair crosses domains (Oxford and the Aztecs, the fax and the telephone, Star Wars and the guillotine), so you reason from anchors instead of recalling one date.
During the reveal the question card shows both dates and the gap (quiz_questions() returns the notes while locked, reveal_ms 2600), so every answer teaches something.
Short tile labels (one line each) keep all tiles at one size; a single hourglass picture fills the middle.
Ranked points with a streak bonus written as two small game rules, lives for a real way to lose.
pitfalls_avoided: Trivia that is pure recall of one fact
A 700 ms reveal nobody can read
Tiles with long labels that shrink to different sizes
An empty middle on the tall canvas

request: a mate in one chess puzzle game where you move the piece that checkmates

brief.intent: chess tactics: find the mating move

themes: chess checkmate mate in one tactics puzzle board game strategy
why_its_good: The player moves the real piece: tap it (legal squares get dots, captures rings) then its square, or drag it; chess_board generates the legal moves in the rules, so every run replays.
Every position was checked with a move generator; any mate counts, not just the listed one.
A wrong move plays out, the card says why it fails (check but the king escapes, or no check), and the piece slides back: no shake, a soft cue and a 20-point penalty. Two misses show the mate.
The 8 x 44 board fills the tall canvas width under a short card, so text never sits on the board.
pitfalls_avoided: Unchecked positions with two mates or none
Turning the board into multiple choice
Coordinate labels crossed by sliding pieces (they sit on plates in the square colour)
